rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Circular motion is described rotationally: **angular displacement** $\theta$ (radians), **angular velocity** $\omega = d\theta/dt$ and **angular acceleration** $\alpha = d\omega/dt$. They convert to linear quantities through the radius: $s = r\theta$, $v = r\omega$, $a = r\alpha$.…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Axis of Rotation Constraint:** Angular quantities ($ heta$, $\omega$, $\alpha$) are defined with respect to a specific fixed axis. If the axis of rotation changes orientation, the angular velocity becomes a time-dependent vector, and simple scalar kinematics no longer apply.  ·  **Kinematic Equations Applicability:** The kinematic equations (analogs of $v = u + at$) for angular motion are strictly valid *only* for constant angular acceleration ($\alpha = ext{constant}$). For time-varying $\alpha(t)$, direct integration of $d\omega/dt$ is required.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Angular velocity points ALONG THE AXIS (right-hand rule), not tangentially — this is the most common confusion.  ·  The kinematic equations for rotation are IDENTICAL in form to linear motion — just swap the variables.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Flywheel 2023*** — r = 0.5 m at 300 rpm: ω = 31.4 rad/s, v = 15.7 m/s.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **rpm vs rad/s:** 300 rpm is 5 revolutions per second = 10π rad/s — always convert before using $v = \omega r$.  ·  **Radian has no dimensions:** angular quantities carry 'rad' as a label, not a base unit — $v = \omega r$ still works dimensionally.

rows.text: Solve 5 problems converting between rpm, rad/s, and revolutions.  ·  Solve 5 problems using the kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Diameter given? Halve it first."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A disc of radius 0.2 m spins at 1200 rpm. Find ω, the rim speed and the period.** — ω = 2π(1200)/60 = 125.7 rad/s; v = ωr = 25.1 m/s; T = 2π/ω = 0.05 s.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Most-tested: rpm→rad/s conversion plus v = ωr (2023, 2024). Expect a_c as a bonus part.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **One conversion unlocks every circular-motion numerical:** $\omega = 2\pi N/60$ turns rpm into rad/s.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: $\theta$ (rad), $\omega = d\theta/dt$ (rad/s), $\alpha = d\omega/dt$ (rad/s²).  ·  $s = r\theta$, $v = r\omega$, $a = r\alpha$; $\omega = 2\pi N/60$ for N rpm.  ·  $T = 2\pi/\omega$, $f = \omega/2\pi$.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Every point of a rigid rotating body shares the same ω, but v = ωr grows with distance from the axis — the rim moves fastest.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Describing Spin A particle moving in a circle is best described by *angle* instead of distance. Angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration are the rotational twins of displacement, velocity and acceleration — and the bridge between them is the radius.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts | Linear (translational) | Angular (rotational) | Relation | |---|---|---| | Displacement $s$ (m) | Angular displacement $\theta$ (rad) | $s = r\theta$ | | Velocity $v$ (m/s) | Angular velocity $\omega$ (rad/s) | $v = r\omega$ | | Acceleration $a$ (m/s²) | Angular acceleration $\alpha$ (rad/s²) | $a = r\alpha$ | **Angular displacement ($\theta$):**…  ·  ## 3. Worked Numericals (NEB 2023, 2024) **Q (4m, 2023):** A flywheel of radius 0.5 m rotates at a constant speed of 300 revolutions per minute. rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Reference Frame:** Angular velocity is defined in an inertial frame. If observing from a rotating reference frame, non-inertial (fictitious) forces like centrifugal or Coriolis forces appear, which must be accounted for if analyzing dynamics in that frame.  ·  Always convert rpm to rad/s before using formulas — forgetting this is the most common calculation error.  ·  The number of revolutions is θ/(2π) — divide angular displacement in radians by 2π.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB frequently asks: 'Find the number of revolutions' — use θ/(2π), not θ in radians.  ·  Note 1: Pay attention to the conditions under which Angular displacement, velocity and acceleration applies  ·  Note 2: Angular displacement, velocity and acceleration connects to multiple other topics in Science
